segments.t: Walking into her assigned room with her bag, Noaf finds herself face to face with Layan's closest allies, Rania and Roqayya. Neither side is thrilled about sharing the space, and Noaf sets firm boundaries right away while the other two whisper uneasily about the washroom. Listen to the whole scene in Jordanian Arabic first.
مش كتير مبسوطة على هاد الوضع.
ما بعرف، بس خلص اسكتي هلأ.
Let's walk through that frosty room welcome one line at a time.
'Hello, girls.' "Marhaba" is the warmest, easiest everyday greeting across Jordan—friendly, casual, and welcome at any hour of the day.
'Just one question, Noaf.' Opening with "bass su'aal", "just a question", almost always signals a pointed challenge rather than polite curiosity.
'How did you end up with us in the same room?' "Sirti" literally means "you became", which Jordanians use just like "how did you end up".
'Answer her, Rania asked you a question.' "Ruddi alayha" literally says "return upon her", the everyday phrasing for "answer her".
'Cut out your cold attitude with us.' "Battli" tells one girl to stop or quit doing something, and "harakaatik" literally means "your moves" or "your antics".
'By the way, I am just like you.' "Ala fikra" literally says "on an idea", and in conversation it works exactly like "by the way" or "for your information".
مش كتير مبسوطة على هاد الوضع.
'I am not very happy about this situation.' "Mabsoota" is one of Levantine Arabic's favorite words for feeling happy, pleased, or content.
'So stay in your own lane and leave me in mine.' Literally, "khalleekom bi-haalkom" says "keep yourselves in your own state"—a crisp way to say "mind your own business".
'Roqayya, do you think she heard everything?' "Tiftikri" asks a woman "do you suppose", and "simiat" means "she heard".
'What do you mean? Which matter exactly?' "Shu qasdik" literally asks "what is your intention", the everyday Jordanian way to ask a girl "what do you mean?".
'I mean the talk that happened in the washroom.' Answering "shu qasdik" with "qasdi"—"my intention is"—mirrors the question word for word.
ما بعرف، بس خلص اسكتي هلأ.

'I do not know, just be quiet now.' Notice "ma baarif" for "I don't know", one of the single most useful phrases you can carry into any Amman conversation. Now let's listen to the whole room scene again.
مش كتير مبسوطة على هاد الوضع.
ما بعرف، بس خلص اسكتي هلأ.
Noaf makes it clear she wants peace and quiet, leaving Rania and Roqayya wondering how much she overheard earlier. Keep an ear out for "ala fikra" when dropping a pointed remark. See you next time.

source.show: مدرسة الروابي للبنات (AlRawabi School for Girls) S1.01
